event-01.question: Who was responsible for robodebt?
event-01.answer:
The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022, was the inquiry that determined who was responsible; its final report is dated 7 July 2023 and its Commissioner was Catherine Holmes AC SC.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022 and chaired by Royal Commissioner Catherine Holmes AC SC, examined who was responsible for the Robodebt scheme.

That Royal Commission delivered its final report on 7 July 2023, containing 57 recommendations (56 numbered, 1 printed without a number).

The commission held 47 hearing transcripts, including a hearing on Day 46 dated 10 March 2023, which are evidence rather than findings.

Kate Thwaites told the House on 7 August 2023 that the report was "a 990-page report that examined the establishment of the scheme and who was responsible for it, and made 57 recommendations".

Bill Shorten told the House on 1 August 2023 that the commission rejected Scott Morrison's evidence as untrue, quoting its findings that "Mr Morrison allowed Cabinet to be misled" and that he "failed to meet his ministerial responsibility to ensure that Cabinet was properly informed".

The same speech records the commission's finding on former minister Alan Tudge, that his release of a recipient's personal details to the media "represented an abuse of that power", and on former minister Stuart Robert, that [n]othing compels ministers to knowingly make false statements.

Mark Dreyfus told the House on 10 October 2024 that the royal commission concluded the former Liberal government's robodebt scheme was a "crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal" and that it was the former government's oversight mechanisms that failed.

Stephen Bates told the House on 8 August 2023 that statements the member for Cook made about the robodebt scheme had been "shown to be false by the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme" and potentially breached privilege.

event-01-run2.question: Who was responsible for robodebt?
event-01-run2.answer:
The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022 and its final report, dated 7 July 2023, was produced under Royal Commissioner Catherine Holmes AC SC.

Zali Steggall told the House on 11 March 2026 that the National Anti-Corruption Commission investigation into the robodebt referrals found two public officials engaged in serious corrupt conduct, while four others, including former prime minister Scott Morrison, were cleared.

The Royal Commission's report set out 57 recommendations (56 numbered, 1 printed without a number) and it made no findings of criminal or civil liability.

Recommendation 10.1, at page 19, states that Services Australia should design its policies and processes with a primary emphasis on the recipients it is meant to serve.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was the inquiry that established responsibility; it was a Commonwealth royal commission established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022 and conducted by Royal Commissioner Catherine Holmes AC SC, reporting on 7 July 2023.

The scheme itself was a 2015 budget measure of the former Coalition government, found unlawful by the Federal Court in late 2019, and the report recorded that the government of the time 'continued to illegally raise debts'.

Mark Dreyfus told the House on 10 October 2024 that the royal commission concluded the former Liberal government's scheme was a 'crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal'.

The Royal Commissioner, Catherine Holmes AC SC, said the scheme 'made many people feel like criminals' and was a costly failure of public administration.

Stephen Bates told the House on 8 August 2023 that statements made by the former Prime Minister and member for Cook on robodebt 'have subsequently been shown to be false by the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme'.

The commission's report made 57 recommendations, including that Services Australia design its policies with primary emphasis on the recipients it is meant to serve.

The commission was established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022 and delivered its final report on 7 July 2023.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022 and its final report was dated 7 July 2023, with Catherine Holmes AC SC named as Royal Commissioner.

The Royal Commission's report loaded 57 recommendations, with 0 government response or implementation documents listed, and 47 hearing transcripts listed as documents, which are evidence rather than findings.

Following the Royal Commission's referrals, the National Anti-Corruption Commission's Operation Myrtleford investigation report, published in March 2026, records 6 findings or opinions and states it makes no recommendations.

In that report, the National Anti-Corruption Commission found that Mr Withnell engaged in corrupt conduct because he knew and intended that automatic default averaging would be central to OCI, and by representing to Mr Kimber and Mr McBride that OCI would not involve averaging he engaged in deliberate conduct designed to mislead them and, through them, DSS.

The National Anti-Corruption Commission found that Ms Wilson engaged in corrupt conduct by intentionally misleading, or attempting to mislead, the Ombudsman, amounting to dishonest performance of her official functions.

The National Anti-Corruption Commission found that Ms Halbert, Ms Musolino, Ms Campbell and Mr Morrison each did not engage in corrupt conduct.

The National Anti-Corruption Commission's Operation Myrtleford report found Mr Withnell engaged in corrupt conduct for deliberately misleading Mr Kimber and Mr McBride about averaging in the scheme's income calculations.

The NACC found Ms Wilson engaged in corrupt conduct by intentionally misleading, or attempting to mislead, the Ombudsman, which amounted to dishonest performance of her official functions.

The NACC cleared Ms Halbert, Ms Musolino, Ms Campbell and Mr Morrison, finding each did not engage in corrupt conduct.

Zali Steggall told the House that the two officials' serious corrupt conduct findings left major unfinished business on robodebt.

The scheme was put forward as a budget measure in 2015 and found unlawful by the Federal Court in late 2019.

The royal commission described robodebt as a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal.

event-01-run4.question: Who was responsible for robodebt?
event-01-run4.answer:
Bill Shorten told the House that hearings had shown the previous government had legal advice that robodebt was unlawful from its start and that Clayton Utz said the scheme could not be justified.

The commission found the scheme was "a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal", and that despite mounting warnings the Government of the time continued to illegally raise debts.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was led by Royal Commissioner Catherine Holmes AC SC, and its report named the scheme's failings; the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC) later found in its Operation Myrtleford investigation report that Mr Withnell and Ms Wilson each engaged in corrupt conduct, while it found Mr Morrison did not.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was established on 18 August 2022 and issued its final report on 7 July 2023, listing 57 recommendations, though 56 are numbered in the report's list and the Australian Government's response refers to 56.

With respect to the referral about Mr Withnell, the NACC stated it was satisfied he engaged in corrupt conduct because he knew and intended automatic default averaging would be central to OCI and, by representing that OCI would not involve averaging, engaged in deliberate conduct designed to mislead Mr Kimber and Mr McBride, and through them DSS, within section 8(1)(a) and alternatively section 8(1)(b) of the NACC Act.

With respect to the referral about Ms Wilson, the NACC stated it was satisfied she engaged in corrupt conduct by intentionally misleading, or attempting to mislead, the Ombudsman, amounting to dishonest performance of her official functions and alternatively their dishonest exercise for the improper purpose of misleading the Ombudsman, within section 8(1)(a) and alternatively section 8(1)(b) of the NACC Act.

The NACC published its Operation Myrtleford investigation report in March 2026, holding 6 findings or opinions, and stated it makes no recommendations.

Catryna Bilyk told the Senate that the Prime Minister was the minister who designed robodebt, the Treasurer who cashed the money from it, and the Prime Minister who refused to fix it.

The National Anti-Corruption Commission's Operation Myrtleford report found Mr Withnell engaged in corrupt conduct by representing the scheme would not involve averaging, and Ms Wilson engaged in corrupt conduct by misleading the Ombudsman.

Zali Steggall told the House in March 2026 that the NACC found two public officials engaged in serious corrupt conduct while four others, including former prime minister Scott Morrison, were cleared.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme published 57 recommendations; it listed 56 numbered recommendations plus one printed without a number in its closing observations.

The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was established by Letters Patent on 18 August 2022, and its final report is dated 7 July 2023.

Bill Shorten moved in the House that it accept the royal commission's findings regarding the former ministers involved in the design and implementation of robodebt.

The report names Catherine Holmes AC SC as the Royal Commissioner.

The Royal Commission's reports make 57 recommendations, and 47 hearing transcripts are held, which are evidence rather than findings.

On 10 August 2023, the House of Representatives voted on a motion to accept the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme's findings, introduced by Maribyrnong MP Bill Shorten, and the majority voted in favour.

Mark Dreyfus told the House the royal commission concluded the former Liberal government's robodebt scheme was a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal.

Don Farrell told the Senate the report set out findings on the Liberal and Nationals' robodebt scheme, which unlawfully raised $1.8 billion of debt against about 435,000 people.

Stephen Bates told the House that the member for Cook's statements on robodebt had been shown to be false by the royal commission.

Brian Mitchell told the House that former Liberal ministers including the member for Cook had offered the defence that they didn't know and nobody told them.

Bill Shorten told the House that the member for Cook claimed he stopped robodebt, and that Stuart Robert had also claimed credit.

sources.snippet: I move: That this House: (1) accepts the findings of the report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme regarding the former ministers involved in the design and implementation of the scheme; (2) expresses its deep regret and apologises to the victims of the unlawful robodebt scheme, and to front-line Centrelink staff; and (3) commits to ensuring this cruel, unlawful chapter in the history of Australian public administration is never repeated. The reason why I'm moving this resolution and the government is supporting it is that we believe that the nation and the parliament cannot move on without accepting a genuine account of what
sources.speaker: Bill Shorten

sources.title: Mark Dreyfus — QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE — 2024-10-10
sources.snippet: I thank the member for Lalor for her question. The robodebt royal commission concluded that the former Liberal government's robodebt scheme was a 'crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal'. This illegal scheme resulted in hundreds of thousands of Australians being served with wrongful debt notices. The royal commissioner, Catherine Holmes AC SC, stated: … made many people feel like criminals. In essence, people were traumatised on the off-chance they might owe money. It was a costly failure of public administration, in both human and economic terms. And with those words, the royal commission summed up the human tragedy that was the
sources.speaker: Mark Dreyfus

sources.title: Don Farrell — QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE — 2023-08-01
sources.snippet: I thank Senator Sheldon for his question and for his deep concern for the impact of robodebt on so many Australians. Yes, I can answer that question because Labor committed to establishing a royal commission into robodebt, and just over 12 months after the government being elected, on the morning of 7 July 2023, Commissioner Holmes delivered her final report for all to see. The report set out its findings on the Liberal and Nationals' cruel robodebt scheme. The report highlighted how the scheme unlawfully raised $1.8 billion of debt against approximately 435,000 vulnerable Australians. The report told the personal stories of tragedy and
sources.speaker: Don Farrell

sources.title: Brian Mitchell — STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS — 2023-08-02
sources.snippet: 'I didn't know. It wasn't my fault. Nobody told me.' That is the defence that former Liberal ministers, including the member for Cook, have been rolling out in the wake of the damning findings of the robodebt royal commission. But they did know, it was their fault and they were told. In January 2017 the then Labor opposition formally requested that the then Prime Minister, Malcolm Turnbull, halt robodebt. The scheme didn't end until November 2019, nearly three years later. sources.title: Bill Shorten — QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE — 2023-08-07
sources.snippet: In recent days there have many who've claimed to have stopped robodebt. Last week, the member for Cook claimed he stopped robodebt. He said: … I closed the scheme down during the operational phases of the scheme when the issues and unintended consequences first arose.
